source.version: arXiv:2409.14634v7, 16 May 2026 (arXiv stamp, p. 1); camera-ready text for ACM CAIS '26 (San Jose, May 26-29, 2026), with the CAIS '26 copyright block and DOI 10.1145/3786335.3813161 on p. 1
source.title_on_document: Scideator: Human-LLM Compound System for Scientific Ideation through Facet Recombination and Novelty Evaluation

supplement.where: Appendices A to H inside this PDF, pp. 11-27 (Appendix Overview on p. 11; p. 10 holds references); no separate online supplement is mentioned
supplement.holds: User-study design, baseline tool, treatment-tool modifications, procedure, and participant demographics (A, pp. 11-12); remaining CSI factor results and participants' own ratings of their favorite ideas' feasibility, specificity, imaginativeness, and impact (B.1, p. 12; Figure 5, p. 13); annotation study (C); retrieval-overlap table (D, Table 3); sample ideas (E, Table 4); implementation details (F); UI and module figures (G); prompt pseudocode (H). No standard errors, standard deviations, or confidence intervals appear anywhere: the CSI is reported as medians with quartiles, and the idea-rating differences as 'M' with quartiles, with M never defined.

paper_design_summary: The user study analyzed 22 computer-science researchers who each completed two 20-minute research-ideation sessions, one with Scideator and one with a paper-selection/free-text baseline using the same LLM (gpt-4o-2024-08-06), in randomized condition order and with randomized topic assignment (p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 11, A.2-A.3). Creativity-related user-study outcomes were participants' self-reports of tool support, favorite-idea qualities, and novelty-assessment confidence; the novelty checker's classifications served as tool feedback and grouping information, with no independent creativity or diversity outcome comparison (pp. 6-7, Sections 4.1.1-4.1.3; p. 12, A.4-A.5). Separate model-only ablations tested novelty-checker retrieval and classification on fixed test sets (pp. 7-8, Section 4.2).

studies.label: Within-subjects user study: Scideator vs paper-level baseline on the same LLM (research ideation)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Order of the two tool conditions (Scideator vs baseline) and which ideation topic went with each condition
assignment.quote: We conducted a within-subjects study, in which each participant completed tasks for the treatment and baseline conditions in randomized order. The ideation topics for the treatment and baseline conditions were also randomized.
assignment.locator: p. 11, Appendix A.2; also p. 6, Section 4.1

arms.name: Scideator (treatment)
arms.description: Facet-based human-LLM ideation system: retrieves analogous papers at four conceptual distances, extracts purpose, mechanism, and evaluation facets, and an LLM (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) recombines user- or system-selected facets into ideas. For the study, on-demand novelty evaluation, manual idea addition, and facet generation without a query were disabled; the novelty checker ran only in a separate novelty-evaluation tab (p. 12, A.4).

arms.name: Baseline (paper-level interaction)
arms.description: The participant selects any of the three input papers and may add free-text custom instructions; the same LLM (gpt-4o-2024-08-06) generates ideas with a simplified prompt that uses no facets; its novelty-evaluation tab gives no novelty-checker output (pp. 11-12, A.3).

participants.exclusions: The paper reports a user-study sample of 22 people, each completing both conditions (p. 3, contributions; p. 6, Section 4.1); no exclusions are reported for CSI or favorite-idea ratings. The CSI test's exact paired analysis count is not stated in p. 6, footnote 5. RQ3 analyzed 17 participants: one participant did not receive the full allotted time and four experienced a different novelty-checker version because of an API issue (p. 7, Section 4.1.3 and footnote 6). In two instances a participant saved only one idea within the allotted time and was asked to select a next favorite idea (p. 12, A.5). The 22 recruited participants are reported in p. 11, A.1, but no separate assignment-stage count is given; n_randomized is therefore null. The two arms contain the same people.
participants.who: Computer-science researchers: 16 PhD students, 5 master's students, 1 industry researcher; 12 HCI and 10 NLP (three of the NLP group focused on other ML areas, p. 6, fn. 4); 7 women, 15 men; all had authored at least one paper; recruited through institutional mailing lists and academic social networks; paid a $60 Amazon gift card
participants.quote: We recruited 22 computer-science researchers (W: 7, M: 15) through institutional mailing lists and academic social networks. We compensated them with a $60 Amazon gift card.
participants.locator: p. 11, Appendix A.1; p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 3, contributions list (N=22)

ai_tool.name_model: Scideator (the authors' system) built on gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (temperature 0.75 in the idea generator); its novelty checker uses SPECTER embeddings, gpt-4o re-ranking, and o3-mini classification. The baseline uses gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with a simplified prompt.
ai_tool.how_used: In both arms an LLM generates research ideas that the participant selects and saves. Scideator: the participant selects facets (or lets the system select them) from input and retrieved analogous papers, and the LLM recombines them into ideas. Baseline: the participant selects input papers and writes optional custom instructions, and the LLM generates ideas directly. A later novelty-evaluation tab offered a ChatGPT-like chat in both tools and the novelty checker's output only in Scideator. The contrast is facet-level vs paper-level interaction with the same LLM, not AI vs no AI.

task.description: Generate and save as many research ideas as possible on an assigned topic (HCI: human-AI collaboration in art, AI tools for education; NLP: dealing with LLM hallucinations, LLM explainability), starting from three assigned input papers; then pick two favorite ideas and rate them; then a separate 5-minute novelty-evaluation task on the two favorites.
task.duration: 20 minutes of idea generation per condition after up to 2 minutes reviewing the input papers, plus 5 minutes of novelty evaluation; each session 105 minutes overall (p. 12, A.5)

outcomes.name: Creativity Support Index (CSI), overall score (0-100)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants' questionnaire ratings of the tool's creativity support (Cherry and Latulipe 2014, ref. [12]), completed after each idea-generation session; rates the experience with the tool, not the ideas. Figure 5a plots each participant's difference in unweighted CSI scores (treatment minus baseline).

contrasts.reported: CSI scores: Scideator median=70.50 (Q1=57.50, Q3=79.00), baseline median=61.00 (Q1=42.25, Q3=71.50). Wilcoxon signed-rank test, V=208.50, p<.01.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1.1 and footnote 5; p. 13, Figure 5a

outcomes.name: Self-rated newness of favorite ideas (7-point)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's own 7-point rating of the newness of their two favorite ideas; no external rater or computed score. The paper does not say which item this is: at saving, participants rated how different the idea was from ideas they had or encountered before the study; after the session they rated each favorite idea's perceived novelty (p. 12, A.5).

contrasts.reported: “participants rated their favorite ideas’ newness on a 7-point scale, showing only a slight advantage for Scideator (median difference: 0.5 points)”; no test statistic or p-value reported

outcomes.name: Self-rated imaginativeness of favorite ideas (7-point)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's own 7-point Likert-type rating of the imaginativeness of their two favorite ideas, averaged; reported as the difference between conditions (Scideator minus baseline) with quartiles.

contrasts.reported: imaginativeness (M=0.00, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.38); M is not defined; no test reported

outcomes.name: Self-rated feasibility, specificity, and impact of favorite ideas (7-point)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three 7-point Likert-type self-ratings of each of the participant's two favorite ideas, averaged; reported as differences between conditions (Scideator minus baseline) with quartiles. Feasibility and impact fit the codebook's usefulness; specificity could also be read as elaboration.

contrasts.reported: feasibility (M=0.00, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.50), specificity (M=0.00, Q1=-0.88, Q3=0.50); “the baseline tool performed slightly better with respect to generating impactful ideas (M=-0.25, Q1=-0.50, Q3=0.00)”; M is not defined; no tests reported

outcomes.name: CSI factor scores (exploration, expressiveness, enjoyment, immersion, results worth effort)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Per-factor CSI ratings of the tool, shown as within-person differences (treatment minus baseline) in box plots with no numbers printed. Text: exploration and expressiveness benefited most; immersion showed no difference; enjoyment slightly favored Scideator with a small difference; results-worth-effort generally favored Scideator. Figure 5c shows how participants ranked the factors' importance.

contrasts.reported: No numbers printed; Figure 5b box plots of factor differences (treatment-baseline). Text: “participants benefited most from Scideator in exploration and expressiveness”; immersion “showed no differences”; enjoyment: “the difference from the baseline was small”.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 4.1.1; p. 12, Appendix B.1; p. 13, Figure 5b

outcomes.name: Perceived novelty of favorite ideas before and after the novelty-evaluation task, and confidence in the novelty assessment (RQ3)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Participants' own 7-point perceived-novelty ratings of their two favorite ideas before and after using the assigned tool's novelty-evaluation tab, grouped by the tool's novelty classification (novel, not novel, none), plus their confidence in their novelty assessment. Tests whether the novelty checker changes participants' assessments, not the creativity of the ideas. The analysis included 17 participants; the paper does not say which paired quantities the sign test compares.

contrasts.reported: Novelty checker “did not significantly improve overall confidence in novelty assessments (sign test, S=5.00, p=n.s.)”; 17 participants analyzed. Figure 4 shows average perceived novelty before and after by the tool's classification, with no numbers printed; participants changed their assessments most when Scideator classified an idea as “not novel”.

studies.label: Novelty-checker ablations (retrieval and classifier) on author-labeled test sets, model only

assignment.what_was_assigned: Not applicable: system variants run on fixed test sets of ideas
assignment.quote: We run two ablations to isolate the contributions of the novelty checker’s main components

participants.who: No human participants. The test sets come from an expert annotation study in which the first two authors labeled 51 ideas (46 generated by Scideator, 5 adapted from OpenReview), yielding 67 consensus-labeled examples (39 novel, 28 not novel) split into an in-context training pool and a held-out test set (p. 5). Retrieval ablation: 58 ideas with known overlapping prior work, 13 held-out 'not novel' ideas plus 45 published NLP papers (p. 7). Classifier ablation: held-out set of 26 novel and 17 not-novel ideas (p. 8).
participants.quote: Our test set contains 58 ideas with known overlapping prior work: 13 “not novel” instances from the held-out set (Section 2) plus 45 published NLP papers.
participants.locator: p. 5, Expert Annotation Study; p. 7, Section 4.2.1; p. 8, Section 4.2.2

ai_tool.how_used: Model-only comparison of retrieval pipelines (Table 1) and classifier prompts (Table 2) for classifying research ideas as novel or not novel

task.description: Classify research ideas as novel or not novel against retrieved literature. Complete-system retrieval accuracy 89.66% vs 5.17% to 13.79% for the ablated variants (p. 8, Table 1); best classifier accuracy 0.81 and macro F1 0.79 (p. 8, Table 2).

company_involvement.description: One co-first author (Simra Shahid) lists Microsoft (Delhi, India) as affiliation; Pao Siangliulue, Tom Hope, and Daniel S. Weld list the Allen Institute for AI. The authors built and evaluate their own system (Scideator). Idea generation in both tools runs on gpt-4o-2024-08-06; the document does not name the model's maker. No funding or acknowledgments statement appears in the PDF.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author block; p. 11, Appendix A.3

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: participants used two generative-AI configurations in randomized within-person order, with topic assignment also randomized (p. 11, A.2-A.3; p. 6, Section 4.1). This is an ai_design comparison. Criterion 2 is not met: the user study analyzed 22 unique people across both conditions (p. 3, contributions; p. 6, Section 4.1), with 17 analyzed for RQ3 after the exclusions in p. 7, footnote 6. Criterion 3 is not met: the CSI measures self-reported tool support, and participants rated their own ideas and their own novelty-assessment confidence (p. 6, Section 4.1; p. 12, A.5). The novelty-checker classifications were tool feedback and grouping information, not an independent creativity/diversity outcome comparison for the randomized study (p. 12, A.4; p. 7, Section 4.1.3). The separately reported retrieval/classifier ablations are model-only (pp. 7-8, Section 4.2). Exclude from core and context evidence; retain in the screening report as a randomized experiment below 50 people with only self-reported creativity-related outcomes.

one_line_finding: In a randomized-order within-subjects study analyzing 22 computer-science researchers, Scideator scored higher than a same-LLM baseline on the self-reported Creativity Support Index (median 70.50 vs 61.00; Wilcoxon V=208.50, p<.01; p. 6, footnote 5), while participants' own ratings of their favorite ideas barely differed (newness median difference 0.5, p. 6, Section 4.1.1; feasibility, specificity, and imaginativeness M=0.00 and impact M=-0.25, p. 12, B.1).
open_questions: Appendix B.1 reports M with quartiles for favorite-idea rating differences but does not define M (p. 12); authors would need to identify the summary statistic.

The reported favorite-idea newness difference (p. 6, Section 4.1.1) is not explicitly linked to either the save-time differentness item or the post-session perceived-novelty item (p. 12, A.5); authors would need to identify the item and aggregation. This is also the unresolved reconciliation difference.

The exact number of paired observations entering the CSI test is not stated (p. 6, footnote 5), although the paper reports N=22 for the user study (p. 3, contributions; p. 6, Section 4.1). Participant-level CSI data and analysis inclusion information would settle this.
The RQ3 sign test (S=5.00, p=n.s.; p. 7, Section 4.1.3) does not identify the paired quantities compared; authors would need to specify the contrast and pairing.
No separate assignment-stage participant count is stated; p. 11, A.1 reports 22 recruited and A.2 describes randomized order. n_randomized remains null pending author confirmation.
notes: No arm works without AI; every contrast is ai_design (two generative-AI configurations on the same LLM). Process measures (facet selection, facet distances, custom-instruction use), interviews, and the authors' annotation study are not outcomes scored on participants' output and are not listed. The number of ideas saved per participant is not reported. Code release is promised “upon acceptance of the paper” (p. 18, Appendix H); no data or code URL is given. The markdown conversion drops minus signs in Appendix A.2 (familiarity Q1=-1.00, p. 11) and B.1 (specificity Q1=-0.88, p. 12); the numbers here follow the PDF. The Appendix Overview (p. 11) labels the prompt section 'G' instead of 'H'. retrieval.json records that earlier arXiv versions of this paper (v1, September 2024) carried a different title. Finalization: the entire markdown, including Appendices A-H, was read; retained screening statistics were checked against PDF text. No c107 challenge files were present, so challenge_resolution and its three counters are empty/zero. Current-spec normalization leaves assignment-stage counts null because the reported 22 is the recruited/user-study count, not a separately reported randomization count. The original claim of 22 plotted markers is not used to establish the CSI test's paired analysis count. The remote supervised sessions remain lab_rct under the codebook's supervised-session definition (p. 12, A.5); this design-label question needs no further source. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged, including its historical count decisions and unresolved newness-item entry.

open_items.item: Undefined M in Appendix B.1 (p. 12): authors must identify whether it denotes a mean, median, or another summary. This affects extraction of self-reported ratings, not any eligibility criterion.

Which item underlies favorite-idea newness (p. 6, Section 4.1.1; p. 12, A.5), also the unresolved reconciliation difference: authors must identify the questionnaire item and aggregation. Both candidate items are self-reports, so neither changes criterion 3; criteria 1 and 2 are unaffected.

Exact CSI paired analysis count (p. 6, footnote 5): participant-level CSI scores and analysis inclusion information would settle it. The reported study sample is only 22 (p. 3, contributions; p. 6, Section 4.1), so this cannot change the failure of criterion 2 or the other criteria.
